transcript.content: Hello, welcome to the clinic. What brings you in to see me today?

Well, it's a bit of a long story, really. I mean, I didn't even think I needed to come here, but my regular doctor, Dr. Henderson—he's been my doctor for about fifteen years now, lovely man, always asks about my cats—he was the one who insisted. I had a check-up a couple of weeks ago, just for my blood pressure medication, and they always make you step on the scale, don't they? I hate that part. Anyway, he got this very serious look on his face and told me I've gotten too thin. He used the word "concerning," actually. And, well, I suppose I can see what he means, physically speaking. I work as a building cleaner over at the community college—have been doing that since my husband passed—and my work pants, the navy blue ones they issue us? They're just hanging off me lately. I have to pull my belt so tight it bunches up the fabric in the back, which is incredibly uncomfortable when I'm bending down to empty the trash bins or mop the hallways. But the thing is... and this is the part I didn't tell Dr. Henderson because I know how it sounds... part of me, a big part of me, actually feels so relieved when I see that number on the scale go down. It's like, I know my pants don't fit and people are looking at me a little funny, but when the number is lower, I just feel this sense of... I don't know, accomplishment? Control? It's confusing, honestly, which I guess is why I'm sitting here talking to you.
When you feel relieved seeing the number on the scale go down, is it because you're afraid of gaining weight?

Well, yes, I suppose that’s a big part of it. It’s funny you use the word afraid, because I don't think of myself as a fearful person, generally speaking. I mean, I work the night shift in empty buildings, and that doesn't bother me one bit. But when it comes to this... yes, there's this underlying dread. It’s just, well, if I eat something heavier, you know? Like, the other day, one of the ladies from the administration office left a tin of biscuits in the breakroom—the really nice buttery ones from Marks & Spencer—and I had one with my tea. Or if I have a small bowl of pasta for dinner instead of just a salad. If I do something like that, I spend the entire rest of the day, or the next day, just absolutely terrified it’s going to show on me. It’s like this nagging voice in the back of my head that won't shut up. I find myself constantly checking the mirror in the ladies' room at work, or looking down at my stomach when I'm sitting down, just to see if it’s suddenly sticking out more. And then I start thinking about how I need to make up for it. I'll tell myself I have to scrub the floors on the entire second level by hand instead of using the machine, or I'll walk the long way home, just to sort of... erase it, I guess? It’s exhausting, really, being so scared of just a little bit of food turning into weight, but I just can't seem to shake the feeling once it starts.
Do you think you look fat even when others tell you that you're too thin?

Well, "fat" is such a harsh word, isn't it? I don't know if I walk around thinking the exact word *fat*, but... well, people do say I'm too thin. Dr. Henderson, obviously, and my sister-in-law Martha—she calls every Sunday evening just to ask what I've eaten, which drives me absolutely up the wall, and she's always saying I'm fading away. But the thing is, when I look at myself, I just don't see what they see. I really don't. 

For me, it's more about being... tidy. I’ve always prided myself on being a tidy person, you know? Keeping a neat house, doing a thorough job at the college, making sure the baseboards are dusted, everything in its proper place. And that extends to my own body. When I stay small and neat, I feel like I'm handling everything right. It’s like, as long as I take up less space and my clothes are loose, my life is in order and I'm coping with everything since my husband passed. 

But if I happen to catch my reflection—like in that big full-length mirror in the faculty restroom on the third floor, the one with that awful, harsh fluorescent lighting that just highlights absolutely every single flaw—if I look in there and my stomach looks the least bit full, even just from drinking a glass of water or having a few bites of something, I just panic. I look at it and I feel like I've completely let myself go. It doesn't matter what Martha or the doctor says about my weight or my BMI or whatever, in that moment, I just feel so sloppy and out of control. I see so many women my age just sort of give up, you know? They start wearing those elastic waistbands and big flowy tunics to hide their middles, and I just... I can't be like that. I refuse to be like that. I can't let myself go. So when they tell me I'm too thin, I always just think, well, you aren't looking at my stomach in the mirror after I've had something to eat, are you? Because if they did, they’d see exactly what I mean.
Is there a specific weight or body shape that you're trying to maintain or achieve?

Well, it's not really a specific number I have written down somewhere, like a goal weight or anything like that. I don't keep a little chart or a diary. It's more of a... a feeling, I suppose? Or a look. Like I was saying about being tidy. I just want to maintain that sense of being compact and neat. 

I remember when I was younger, before I had my daughter—she lives in Seattle now, by the way, works in software, very busy, we talk on Sundays but she's always rushing off to some meeting or another—anyway, before I had her, I was always very slender. I wore a size four, sometimes a two in certain brands, and I always felt so put-together. Then, of course, life happens, you get older, and things shift. But after Arthur died... I don't know. I just started noticing how much better I felt when I was smaller. 

So, I don't step on the scale every morning thinking, "I must weigh exactly this many pounds." It's more about how my clothes fit, how my stomach feels when I press my hand against it, whether I can feel my collarbones when I'm washing my face in the morning. If I can feel them, if they feel sharp and distinct, then I know I'm doing okay. I know I haven't let things slip. If I wake up and I feel sort of... soft, or puffy, well, that just ruins the whole day. I'll spend my entire shift at the college just distracted, thinking about how I need to fix it. So I guess the shape I'm trying to maintain is just... empty. Neat, compact, and empty. Does that make sense? It's not a number, it's just a state of being where I feel like I'm not taking up too much room.
Did your fear of gaining weight start after your husband passed away?

Well, Arthur’s passing... that was five years ago this coming November. It was very sudden, you know. We were just sitting in the living room, and... well, anyway. I suppose you could say that’s when things really took a turn. Before he died, I never really obsessed over every little thing I put in my mouth. But after he was gone, the house was just so terribly quiet. I actually took this night shift job at the college just to keep myself occupied, to get out of that empty house. 

And that fear I was telling you about earlier? It really did take root then. Like I mentioned before with those buttery biscuits in the breakroom, or having a proper bowl of pasta—it’s like, ever since Arthur died, if I eat something heavier like that, the anxiety just absolutely consumes me. I spend the entire rest of the day, sometimes the next two days, just terrified it’s going to instantly show on my body. I’ll be buffing the floors in the main hall, and I’ll catch my reflection in the big glass doors, and I just stop and check myself, over and over, turning sideways to see if my stomach is sticking out. 

And then my mind just races with all the ways I need to make up for it. I’ll tell myself I have to do the stairs in the science building twice, or scrub the grout in the restrooms until my knuckles ache. It’s just... when Arthur died, I couldn't control any of it. The whole world just fell out from under me and it was completely out of my hands. So now, if I eat something dense or heavy, I just get so incredibly scared that I'm losing my grip on this, too. I just have to do whatever it takes to make sure the food doesn't show on me. I just can't bear the thought of it.
Do you think you look different from how others see you?

Well, I suppose I must, mustn't I? Because, like I was trying to explain earlier about Martha and Dr. Henderson... they look at me and they see someone who is, I don't know, fading away, or someone who is unwell. But I just don't see that. When I look at myself, it's entirely different. 

It really goes back to what I was saying about being tidy. When I look in the mirror and I see that I've stayed small and neat, I don't see a sick person at all. I see a woman who is handling everything right. I see someone who is keeping her life together, keeping all the pieces from scattering everywhere like they did when Arthur passed. I see someone who is disciplined and put-together. 

But then... oh, it's just so frustrating because people don't understand how quickly that image changes for me. If I have a glass of water, or if I eat something and then I happen to catch my reflection—like in that awful faculty restroom mirror, or even just the reflection in the glass of the display cases in the history department while I'm dusting them—if my stomach looks the least bit full, I don't see what Martha sees at all. I don't see someone who's "too thin." I just look at that little bit of roundness, that tiny bulge, and I feel like I've completely let myself go. I feel like a total failure in that moment, like I'm just sloppy and undisciplined and all my hard work of keeping things neat has just vanished. 

And I try to tell Martha this! I say, "Martha, you just aren't seeing me right after I've eaten, you aren't seeing how my stomach pushes out against my slacks," but she just sighs at me. She doesn't get it. She doesn't understand that the way I look to myself in those moments is just... it's unbearable. So yes, I do think we're seeing two completely different things. They see a number on a scale, I suppose, but I just see whether or not I'm keeping my life in order.
Do you think your weight is actually lower than what the scale says it is?

Well, it's funny you mention the scale, because... well, Dr. Henderson, my general practitioner, he's always telling me I've gotten too thin. He looks at my chart and shakes his head, and he's got this very serious tone he uses, like he's talking to a child who won't listen. And, you know, I do see what he means, in a practical sense. Like with my work uniform. The college issues us these heavy navy blue slacks—awful material, really stiff and unforgiving—and lately, they're just hanging off me. I have to pull my belt so tight that the fabric bunches up all around the waist, and it looks terrible, just so untidy. I spend half my shift hiking them up while I'm trying to mop the hallways. 

So I know, logically, that the number on the scale must be low. I know I've lost weight. But... and this is the part that's so hard to explain to Dr. Henderson or to Martha... when I actually step on the scale in my bathroom—it's this old digital one Arthur bought years ago, the battery cover is held on with a piece of scotch tape—when I look down and see that the number is lower, I don't feel worried. I don't think, "Oh dear, my pants won't fit." I just feel... relieved. It's this immense, washing wave of relief. It's like a little confirmation that I'm doing it right, that I'm keeping everything contained. 

Even if the doctor says it's too low, and even if my clothes are falling off, that lower number just feels like a victory. It feels safe. So I don't think the scale is lying, exactly, or that I weigh less than it says... it's just that what the scale says means something completely different to me than it does to anyone else. To them, it's a warning sign. To me, it's just... it's proof that I haven't let go of the reins.
Do you think you would still be afraid of gaining weight if you couldn't see your body?

Oh, well... I suppose... I don't think taking away the mirrors would really change anything, to be completely honest with you. Because, you see, it’s not just about the physical act of looking, even though I know I just went on and on about checking my reflection in the glass doors and the bathroom mirrors. It’s the knowing. It’s that heavy feeling inside. 

Like I was trying to explain just a little bit ago, and I know I keep coming back to this, but if I eat something heavier, like one of those biscuits from the breakroom or a bowl of pasta... even if I were in a pitch-black room and couldn't see a thing, I would still spend the entire rest of the day just absolutely scared to death that it’s going to show on me. 

Because even if I couldn't see my body with my eyes, my mind would still be doing the exact same thing. I'd still be checking myself, just in different ways. I'd be feeling my stomach with my hands underneath my uniform, or pressing my arms tight against my sides while I'm emptying the trash bins, just desperately trying to gauge if I've gotten bigger or softer. The terror of it doesn't just vanish because I can't see it. I’d still be standing there thinking that I need to make up for it, feeling that awful, urgent pressure telling me I have to go scrub the baseboards in the library until my shoulders ache, or walk the perimeter of the campus just to be sure I'm fixing it. So, no, not seeing my body wouldn't stop the fear at all. The fear just takes over the second I swallow something dense, whether I can see myself or not.
Do you think your fear of gaining weight is because you believe you would look unattractive if you gained weight?

Unattractive? Oh... no, I wouldn't use that word. It really isn't about being pretty or trying to look like some model in a magazine, if that's what you're getting at. I mean, I'm sixty-four years old and I spend my evenings scrubbing floors and wiping down chalkboards—people don't really look twice at the cleaning lady anyway, do they? We're practically invisible in those big university buildings. And I certainly aren't trying to catch anyone's eye. Arthur was my only love, and since he passed, well, vanity just hasn't been any sort of priority for me. 

So, no, it's not about attractiveness at all. It’s really exactly what I was trying to explain to you earlier, when we were talking about catching my reflection in the glass. I know I'm repeating myself a bit here, but it really just boils down to keeping things in order. When I make sure that I stay small and neat, I feel like I'm handling everything right. It’s like I have this tight grip on my life, keeping everything perfectly structured and tidy, just like how I have to organize my supply cart before a shift so the cleaning solutions don't spill. 

But the second I see any change... if I look in the mirror and my stomach looks the least bit full, even if it's just from drinking a cup of tea or having a piece of toast in the breakroom, I don't think, "Oh dear, I look ugly." I just feel like I've completely let myself go. It’s this overwhelming, crushing sense of failure, like I've become sloppy and careless, just like the students who leave their rubbish shoved into the cracks of the lecture hall seats. 

If I gain weight, it means I'm losing that discipline. It means I'm not doing my job of holding myself together. So the fear isn't about being unattractive to other people, it’s about that horrible, panicky feeling of unraveling, of not being neat and contained anymore. To me, being small is just... it's being capable. It's proof that I haven't let the mess win.
Do you feel like gaining weight would mean you're losing control of your life?

Yes, exactly. I know I just touched on that a moment ago, but that is really the absolute heart of it, isn't it? Control. That's a very good word for it. Because, you see, after Arthur passed away, everything in my life just felt so... unmoored. Like it was all just floating away from me. The house suddenly felt entirely too big and too quiet, the bank statements were confusing, and I took this job at the university just to have somewhere to be, just to have something to do with my hands so I wouldn't sit in his armchair all day. 

And every evening I go in there, and I see these young students rushing around, spilling their coffees, leaving scuff marks all over the freshly waxed linoleum in the science building... it's just constant chaos. It's a constant, never-ending mess that other people make, and I'm the one who has to quietly follow behind and put it all back to rights. 

So my own body... well, it’s the one thing, perhaps the very only thing left in my life, that I can keep perfectly in line. Like I was saying before, when I manage to stay small and neat, I feel like I'm handling everything right. I feel like I'm steering the ship, so to speak. It tells me that I haven't succumbed to the chaos. 

But the absolute second I step out of the shower and catch a glimpse of myself, if my stomach looks the least bit full in the mirror... oh, Doctor, it's just devastating. I don't just see a physical change. I feel like I've completely let myself go. I feel like I'm becoming just as careless and sloppy as the people who leave their trash on the library tables. If I were to actually gain weight, it would mean the mess had finally won. It would mean I wasn't capable of managing myself anymore. So, yes, keeping the weight off is... it's the only way I know I'm still holding on to the reins.
Do you think your body is larger than it actually is when you're afraid of gaining weight?

Well... larger than it actually is? I suppose... I mean, it’s a difficult thing to explain, and I know I keep circling back to this same point, but it really all comes down to what I see when I catch my reflection while I'm working. 

It’s like... well, when I stay small and neat, I look in the glass and I just feel this immense relief. I look at my reflection and I feel like I'm handling everything right, like I'm keeping all the pieces of my life tucked in exactly where they belong. It looks correct to me. It looks safe. 

But if I get scared that I've gained weight... say I've had a glass of water or a few bites of a sandwich in the breakroom... the way I see myself completely shifts. I know, logically, that a few bites of food don't add ten pounds in five minutes. I went to college for a couple of years, I'm not a foolish woman. I understand how biology works. But when that panic sets in, my eyes just lock onto my midsection, and if my stomach looks the least bit full in the mirror, it doesn't just look like a normal stomach anymore. It looks... it looks enormous to me. It feels like it’s just protruding and taking up all this space, completely out of proportion with the rest of me. 

And it’s in those moments, standing there under those harsh fluorescent lights in the staff restrooms, staring at that fullness... I just feel like I've completely let myself go. It feels like this massive, glaring evidence that I've lost my grip and become sloppy. Even if my uniform still buttons exactly the same way it did that morning, what I actually see in the mirror is this huge, heavy failure. It just expands in my mind until it's all I can focus on. So, yes, I do think I see it as much larger than it probably is, because the fear just distorts everything until all I can see is the mess I'm making of myself.
Do you think your body shape or weight is different from how it actually is when you look in the mirror?

Well, I know I must be sounding like a broken record at this point, Doctor, because it feels like we're circling right back to the exact same thing again. But... yes. Shape, weight, size... it all just gets so terribly twisted up in my head when I stand in front of that glass. 

Like I was trying to explain just a moment ago, it all hinges on that reflection. As long as I can look in the mirror in the staff washroom and see that my shape is small and... well, tidy, I suppose... it just gives me this profound sense of relief. It reassures me that I'm doing things correctly. When I'm small and neat, it tells me I'm handling everything right in my life, that I'm keeping the chaos at bay. The shape I see when I'm empty is the shape of a woman who has her life properly organized. 

But if I catch my reflection and there's even the slightest shift—if my stomach seems even a tiny bit rounder, or if I imagine my waist isn't perfectly straight—it’s not just a minor physical change I'm seeing. The shape itself looks completely wrong to me. It looks heavy and cumbersome, and I immediately get that awful, sinking feeling that I've just completely let myself go. Even if the tag on my work slacks says they're the exact same size they were yesterday, the shape I see in the mirror is the shape of a woman who has given up, who is sloppy and careless. 

My mind just takes that tiny bit of fullness and magnifies it until it's the only thing I can see, and it completely overtakes the reality of what's actually there. I'll stand there rubbing a smudge off the mirror with my rag, just staring at myself, and the shape I see is absolutely dictated by that fear. So, yes, I suppose the shape I see is completely different from reality, because it's so tied up in whether I feel neat and capable, or whether I feel like I've let the mess win.
Do you think your fear of gaining weight is because you have a distorted view of what you look like?

Well, I suppose that’s... I mean, yes, but it’s more than just a distorted view, isn't it? It’s not just that my eyes are playing tricks on me, it’s what that view actually means for my entire life. I know we keep coming back to this, and I apologize for going on and on, but it really is the crux of the whole matter. 

You see, it’s not just about looking in the mirror and seeing a different size. It’s about the feeling that comes with it. When I’m at work, pushing that heavy cart down the long, empty hallways of the science building late at night, and I catch a glimpse of myself in one of the glass doors... if I see that I'm staying small and neat, it just washes this wave of calm over me. It’s like I can take a deep breath and say to myself, "You're doing okay, Eleanor. You're keeping it together." I feel like I'm handling everything right. It’s the one piece of evidence I have that I haven't just completely fallen apart since Arthur died. 

But if I look in that same glass door and my stomach looks the least bit full... if I perceive even the slightest bit of extra weight or roundness... the panic is just immediate and overwhelming. It’s not just, "Oh, I look a bit heavier today." It’s this absolute certainty that I have failed. I feel like I've completely let myself go. I feel like I'm turning into one of those careless people who just leave their messes for someone else to clean up. 

So the fear of gaining weight... yes, it’s tied to how I see myself, but it’s because how I see myself dictates whether I feel like a capable, organized human being, or whether I feel like a total disaster. The distortion isn't just in the mirror, Doctor, it's in what that reflection tells me about my worth and my ability to survive in this world without everything falling to pieces.
Do you feel like gaining weight would mean you're not just losing control of your body, but also of your emotions or other aspects of your life?

Well, yes... exactly that. I know I must sound like a broken record today, and I really do apologize for going on and on about the exact same feeling, but you’ve just hit the nail right on the head. That is exactly what it is. 

It’s like I was saying before... when I manage to stay small and neat, I look at myself and I just feel like I'm handling everything right. It’s not just about my waistline. It means my mind is clear, my emotions are neatly folded away, my bills are paid... I'm keeping the chaos out. I spend my entire night shift cleaning up after college students and professors, scrubbing their floors and emptying their overflowing trash bins. And as long as I stay small, I am the one controlling the mess. I am not the mess myself. 

But... oh, if I catch a glimpse in the mirror and my stomach looks the least bit full... it’s terrifying, because it doesn't just mean I need a larger size in my work slacks. It means the control is gone. I feel like I've completely let myself go, in every possible sense of the word. I start thinking that if I can't even keep my own body tidy and disciplined, then my whole life is going to fall apart. I worry my grief over Arthur is just going to spill out all over the place, or that I'll start making mistakes at work, or that I'll just become this sloppy, careless woman who can't manage her own life. 

So, yes, the weight... it’s not just flesh, Doctor. It’s the physical proof of whether I’m holding my life together or whether I’m completely losing my grip on everything. If the body gets out of control, the rest of it is sure to follow right behind it.
Do you believe that gaining weight would cause you to lose control over your emotions?

I know we are circling the drain on this exact same point, Doctor, and I really do apologize because I feel like I'm just saying the same thing to you over and over again today. But... yes, absolutely. My emotions are entirely wrapped up in it. 

It's like a physical containment, you see? Like I've been saying, when I stay small and neat, I feel like I'm handling everything right. And "everything" absolutely includes all those heavy, messy feelings. The grief over Arthur, the quietness of the house, the anxiety of getting older... as long as my body is small and disciplined, those emotions stay neatly tucked away where they belong. It's just like the sorted recycling bins I take out to the loading dock every night at the university. Everything has its proper place, and as long as I'm keeping myself tidy, I'm keeping my feelings tidy, too.

But the very second I look in the mirror and my stomach looks the least bit full... oh, it's just this immediate, terrifying floodgate opening. I feel like I've let myself go, and if I've let my physical self go, then my emotions are just going to spill out everywhere for the whole world to see. I think about being at work, just me and the hum of the floor buffing machine in those empty corridors... if I were to gain weight, if I were to lose that shape, I just know I'd be standing there crying over my mop bucket. I'd be a weeping, hysterical mess because the one thing keeping me anchored, the one thing keeping the sadness in check, would be gone. 

If my stomach gets round, the sadness gets big. The fear gets big. It's all connected. So, yes, if I were to gain weight, I firmly believe my emotions would just run entirely amok. I wouldn't be able to hold back the tears or the panic anymore, because I wouldn't have that physical proof that I'm still capable of holding it all together.
Do you believe that gaining weight would cause you to lose control over your emotions?

Well, Doctor, I know I'm just repeating myself at this point, and I do apologize for talking your ear off about the exact same thing, but... yes. It's exactly what I was just saying. I really can't separate the physical shape of my body from my emotional state anymore. They are entirely intertwined. 

You see, it all comes back to that visual check I was telling you about. I spend so much of my time alone in those university buildings. Just me, my cleaning cart, and the quiet of the night. And when I catch sight of myself in the reflective glass of the lecture halls, or the big mirrors in the third-floor restrooms—I always scrub those last, usually around two in the morning—when I see that I'm staying small and neat, I feel like I'm handling everything right. It’s a very specific, very deep kind of relief. I can look at my reflection in my uniform and think, "Okay, Eleanor, you're holding it together. The grief isn't winning today. You are keeping the mess on the outside." 

But... if I look in that exact same mirror and my stomach looks the least bit full... oh, it's just devastating. It's not just a passing thought. I feel like I've let myself go, completely and utterly. And that’s when the emotions just threaten to take over and swallow me whole. If my stomach is full, it means the discipline is gone, and if the discipline is gone, what’s to stop me from just collapsing right there on the freshly mopped linoleum and crying until I can't breathe? The sadness over losing Arthur, the anxiety about getting older all by myself in that quiet house... it’s all kept in check by staying small. 

If my body takes up more space, the emotions take up more space, and I just... I can't let that happen. I wouldn't survive it. So, yes, the weight and the feelings, they are the exact same thing to me. I have to stay neat to keep the feelings neat.
Do you think your fear of gaining weight is because you have a distorted view of your own body shape or size?

Distorted... well, now, I don't know if I would use the word distorted, Doctor. That makes it sound like I'm looking into one of those funhouse mirrors at a carnival, seeing things that aren't really there. But I know what I see. I mean, I'm the one who cleans those mirrors on the campus. I use the industrial glass cleaner, I wipe them down with the microfiber cloths until there's not a single streak or smudge left, so I know for a fact that the reflection looking back at me is perfectly clear and accurate. 

I know I just keep coming back to this exact same point, and I really do appreciate your patience with an old woman who can't seem to stop talking in circles today, but it all just boils down to what I was just telling you. When I look in that perfectly clean glass, and I see that I've managed to stay small and neat, I feel like I'm handling everything right. It doesn't feel like a distortion. It feels like the absolute, undeniable truth. It feels like I am succeeding at keeping the mess away.

But... if I'm standing there, maybe taking a quick breather by the sinks on the second floor, and I look in the mirror and my stomach looks the least bit full... I feel like I've let myself go. And I mean I feel it in my very bones. I don't look at it and think, "Oh, Eleanor, that's just a distortion, you're imagining things." No, I look at it and I see failure. I see a woman who is losing her grip. 

Maybe other people would look at me and say I'm making a mountain out of a molehill, or that my eyes are playing tricks on me. But to me, that fullness is as real as the mop in my hands. If there is even a fraction of an inch of extra roundness there, my whole perception of myself just completely shatters. I don't see a woman who just drank a glass of water or had a bite to eat. I see a sloppy, careless person. So, no, I don't think it's a distorted view. I think it's just... it's the reality of how thin the line is between me holding my life together and me completely falling apart.
Do you believe that gaining weight would mean you are unable to cope with the challenges of your daily life?

Oh, Doctor, I feel dreadful because I'm just circling right back to the exact same thing again. You must think I only have one thought in my lonely old head, and I know I'm taking up so much of your time with my rambling today, but... yes. Yes, that's exactly it. Coping with my daily life is the whole battle, isn't it? 

People think my life is simple now, but it's really not. Waking up in that desperately quiet house without Arthur, making my tea for one, putting on my heavy work uniform, driving to the campus in the pitch dark, dealing with the bills, the endless silence... all of those things are my daily challenges. And just like I've been saying to you all afternoon, my ability to handle every single one of those things is completely, entirely tied to my size. 

It's just as I was explaining before—when I stay small and neat, I feel like I'm handling everything right. I feel equipped to push my heavy cart down those long corridors, to empty the bins, to just get through another night on my own. I feel capable. But if I happen to catch my reflection in the glass of the double doors by the science lab, and if my stomach looks the least bit full in the mirror... well, I feel like I've let myself go. 

And if I've let myself go physically, how on earth am I supposed to cope with everything else? It feels like the wheels would just fall right off the wagon. If I can't even keep my own body disciplined and tidy, I certainly wouldn't be able to handle the grief or the loneliness or even just the basic tasks of my job. The weight is the only thing I have a strict handle on. So if I were to gain weight, yes, I firmly believe I wouldn't be able to cope with a single thing in my life anymore. It would all just fall apart.
